title: How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
titleZh: 亚马逊如何推高整个互联网的价格
author: sighborg
relevanceReason: 命中 3 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition. But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because...💙 AmandaLast week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over: the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop.In a nutshell, here's what's happening:

This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon.Let's get into it.Amazon charges sellers a lot of feesAmazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales. But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half!Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top.
Where an Amazon sale goes Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising.

There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article.Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice. Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options:

In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising. So, sellers have to raise pricesHere's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices.Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too.And they can't charge less elsewhereNow here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller, if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales.The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon.It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit, California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target. Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go. There's no easy way outFor sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales. For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option.At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon, arguing that it illegally maintains its monopoly power by, among other things, punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere, effectively forcing them to use its warehouses and charging ever-higher fees. Amazon denies any wrongdoing, and the case is set to go to trial next year. In Europe, Germany ordered Amazon to stop controlling its sellers' prices earlier this year, though the decision isn't yet final.After last week's piece, a Not-Ship reader wrote to say none of this is new: plenty of online stores push ads and fake discounts. That is true. But what's different about Amazon is its reach. When prices increase on Amazon, they tend to increase elsewhere too. You can, of course, choose not to shop on Amazon. But if the FTC is right, you may be paying Amazon's prices anyway.

comments.author: steveBK123
comments.textRawHtml:
I find that 20 years ago I shopped at Amazon for the low prices, but 2020s+ I shop at Amazon due to their logistics.

The problem for everyone else is not simply that Amazon ships quickly, I almost don't even care about that. The thing is that Amazon ships & delivers on a reliable predicted schedule. When I click an item on Amazon and it says "arrives by Tuesday" then 95/100 times it does. I shop at specific competitors who can do similar (B&H, Sweetwater, etc).

Many online stores big & small in the year 2026 will still take days to even send shipment info, followed by using unreliable carriers that miss ETAs.

I would even be OK with these stores giving a narrow range or probability "90% of the time this arrives between Tuesday & Wednesday".. But I am not in the mood to order stuff that may arrive in 2-10 days with very little clarity on which end of the range.
comments.textZhHtml:
我发现 20 年前我在亚马逊购物是因为价格低廉，但 2020 年代以后我在亚马逊购物是因为他们的物流。

其他人的问题不仅仅是亚马逊发货速度快，我什至几乎不关心这一点。 问题是亚马逊按照可靠的预测时间表发货和交付。 当我点击亚马逊上的一件商品时，它说“周二到货”，那么有 95/100 次是这样。 我在可以做类似操作的特定竞争对手（B&H、Sweetwater 等）处购物。

到 2026 年，许多大大小小的在线商店仍然需要几天时间才能发送发货信息，然后使用错过预计到达时间的不可靠承运商。

我什至可以接受这些商店给出的狭窄范围或概率“90% 的时间在周二和周三之间到达”。 2-10 天，对于该范围的哪一端还不太清楚。

children.author: CrimsonRain
children.textRawHtml:
And then return...

Got a dud? Quality not as expected? Ordered two by mistake? Size is not fitting? Take it to nearest post office, scan a qr code and hand it over. Done.

The other day I had to pack a product not bought from Amazon, then drive 25 minutes to a specific company's drop off point at some weird opening hours...

And that's after it took me to write manual email to get return label...the entire process took multiple weeks. And then a few more weeks until getting the refund.

At this point, I'm happy to pay 10% extra just to buy from Amazon.
children.textZhHtml:
然后返回...

有一个哑弹？质量不及预期？错订了两个？尺寸不合适？将其带到最近的邮局，扫描二维码并将其交给。完成。

前几天，我不得不打包一件不是从亚马逊购买的产品，然后在一些奇怪的营业时间开车 25 分钟到特定公司的投递点...

那是在我手动编写电子邮件以获得退货标签之后...整个过程花了数周时间。然后再过几周才能收到退款。

此时，我很乐意支付 10% 的额外费用才能从亚马逊购买。

children.textRawHtml: The one issue here is that to achieve this result and make the customer king (or spoiled child, you choose), they exploit and abuse absolutely everyone else, people and partners.
children.textZhHtml: 这里的一个问题是，为了实现这一结果并让客户为王（或者是被宠坏的孩子，你可以选择），他们绝对剥削和虐待其他所有人、人和合作伙伴。

children.author: OroPla
children.textRawHtml:
I'm a customer, though, not the moral police. I don't have the time, energy or inclination to screen every company before buying from them.

Everyone large enough will have a few disgruntled people making up bad things that might or might not be true. In the case of amazon, the few claims I followed up on turned out to be exaggerated or false.
children.textZhHtml:
不过，我是一名顾客，而不是道德警察。我没有时间、精力或意愿在从每家公司购买产品之前对其进行筛选。

每个足够大的公司都会有一些心怀不满的人编造坏事，这些坏事可能是真的，也可能不是真的。就亚马逊而言，我跟进的一些说法结果被证明是夸大或错误的。

children.textRawHtml: That’s the moment we need to show some morality and empathy.
children.textZhHtml: 这就是我们需要表现出一些道德和同理心的时刻。

The issues with the monopoly are true, but in this instance I am happy to pay a bit more and not to be vulnerable to fake sites, dodgy sellers who do not replace an obviously bad product and the like

children.author: IAmBroom
children.textRawHtml:
> Directly ordering in china even offers better customer support

That is 180-degrees off of my experience.

Chinese sellers go so far as to actually claim they are US or UK sellers, right up until you have to return something. I bought a size 6-1/2 blue hat; they shipped a size 7 black hat; the return mail to China ("We're a USA company!") would have cost me 75% of the initial purchase.

I protested to Discover; they eventually decided I ordered what I got (WHAT???), and sided with the seller.
children.textZhHtml:
> 在中国直接订购甚至可以提供更好的客户支持

这与我的经验大相径庭。

中国卖家甚至声称自己是美国或英国卖家，直到你必须退货。我买了一顶 6-1/2 号的蓝色帽子；他们发货了一顶 7 号的黑色帽子；退回到中国的邮件（“我们是一家美国公司！”）将花费我最初购买的 75%。

我向 Discover 提出抗议；他们最终决定我订购了我得到的东西（什么？？？），并站在卖家一边。

children.author: mchusma
children.textRawHtml: I agree, returns are where amazon crushes it. I feel like there should be some startup just focusing on making the perfect returns product for small brands. Just do anything including at home pickup and then figure out how to optimize later.
children.textZhHtml: 我同意，退货是亚马逊压垮它的地方。我觉得应该有一些初创公司专注于为小品牌提供完美的回报产品。只需做任何事情，包括上门取货，然后再考虑如何优化。

children.author: yz453
children.textRawHtml:
Fwiw, Amazon also offers sellers return as a service. Sellers do not need to onboard to Amazon logistics to use the return service. Ofc someone has to pay for that.

Taking returned items from customers is only the beginning of the process. The real difficulties show up after that. Which of the returns can be sold as new, which can be sold as-is, and which can be repaired / refurbished. What if a unit is returned once again? Did the customer return counterfeit? How to detect bad-faith actors (which may be the seller)? Who is to blame for damages? What if the item requires special handling (household chemicals, batteries, etc.)? And how to safely dispose / liquidate inventory while being compliant to all the regulations? And, imagine adding taxes, revenues, fees, on top of all that.

A lot of these questions are very labor-intense. It may be possible to automate some bits here and there, but the complexity is inherent to the problems.

It'd be really hard to imagine a random startup can handle returns half as well. Amazon's regulatory compliance team is probably many times larger than a random average startup. Here the economies of scale is really in favor of the big players.
children.textZhHtml:
Fwiw，亚马逊还为卖家提供退货服务。卖家无需通过亚马逊物流即可使用退货服务。 Ofc 必须有人为此付费。

从客户处收取退回的物品只是整个流程的开始。真正的困难在那之后才显现出来。哪些退货可以作为新产品出售，哪些可以按原样出售，哪些可以修理/翻新。如果单位再次被退回怎么办？顾客退回的是假货吗？如何检测恶意行为者（可能是卖家）？谁该为损害负责？如果该物品需要特殊处理（家用化学品、电池等）怎么办？以及如何在遵守所有法规的同时安全地处置/清算库存？而且，想象一下除此之外还要增加税收、收入、费用。

其中很多问题都非常耗费人力。也许可以在这里或那里实现一些自动化，但复杂性是问题所固有的。

很难想象随机启动的公司也能处理一半的回报。亚马逊的监管合规团队可能比随机的平均初创公司大很多倍。在这里，规模经济确实有利于大企业。

children.author: markdown
children.textRawHtml:
That model started in South America. They're called Bin Stores.

One day a week the bins fill up with returned/liquidated goods from Amazon, Target, etc etc. Everything in the bin is the same price and the price drops every day until they fill up again a week later.

Search "bin store" on youtube or tiktok and you should get a million videos about the craze.
children.textZhHtml:
该模式始于南美洲。它们被称为“Bin Stores”。

每周有一天，这些垃圾箱会装满来自亚马逊、Target 等公司的退货/清算商品。垃圾箱中的所有商品价格都相同，而且价格每天都会下降，直到一周后再次装满。

在 YouTube 或 Tiktok 上搜索“Bin Store”，您应该会看到一百万个有关这股热潮的视频。
